blurb: Thread-fine stems carrying nodding violet-blue bells that shiver in any breeze — delicate to look at and the toughest plant on CSU's whole list, growing as a landscape plant to 13,000 ft. It takes most soils and blooms from midsummer to frost.
water: Low to moderate; occasional deep soak in summer heat
spread: Slender clump, spreading slowly by thin rhizomes and seed
seasons: Nodding violet-blue bells midsummer to frost on thread-fine stems; narrow delicate foliage; dies back in winter
wildlife: Native bees and butterflies work the flowers

care.hardiness: CSU lists this as a Colorado native plantable to about 13,000 ft, so cold is not the constraint at Boulder's zone 5b–6a.[1]
care.planting: Plant in spring after the mid-May last frost, or in early fall, into ground prepared to suit it (see Soil). Set out young container plants — most of these natives resent having an established root system disturbed — and water them in well, then taper off.[1][2]
care.sun: Full sun to part shade, which is CSU's exposure rating for it.[1]
care.soil: Most soils, per CSU. That tolerance is unusual on this list and makes it one of the easier natives to place, though it still prefers drainage over standing wet.[1]
care.water: Low to moderate. CSU rates its moisture requirement low to moderate, and on the semi-arid Front Range that is the number that matters most — the commonest way to kill a xeric native here is kindness with the hose.[1][2]
care.spacing: Space to suit its mature spread of 8–12 in wide. Narrow delicate foliage under nodding bell-shaped flowers — and CSU rates it for most soils, to 13,000 ft, the highest planting elevation on its list.[1]
care.propagation: By seed, which is how nearly all of these natives are raised and how they persist in a planting. Autumn sowing outdoors lets winter provide the chilling most of them want.[1]
care.bloom: Flowers from midsummer through to frost; CSU records the colour as purple, blue and the height as 8–15 in tall.[1]
care.maintenance: Low. Cut old growth back in late winter or early spring rather than in fall, so the stems hold snow and give the crown some cover. Skip fertilizer: lean soil keeps these natives compact and long-lived.[1][2]
care.troubles: Few pests or diseases when it is sited right. Crown and root rot in soil that stays wet is the usual cause of failure for a Colorado native in a Front Range garden, and it is a siting problem rather than bad luck.[1][2]

edible.summary: No documented culinary use in the authorities consulted; grown as an ornamental native.[1]
edible.caution: No authority consulted documents a food use for harebell, so this guide treats it as inedible — don't eat it. Some other bellflowers do have a food record (the roots of rampion, *Campanula rapunculus*, for instance), but that belongs to a different species and this guide does not extend it to harebell.[1]
